subject: biology
prompt: Sugarcane plants in a field look almost the same. But people in a crowd look very different from one another. What is the best reason for this?

image.alt: Identical sugarcane plants beside a group of very different people

options.text: Sugarcane plants have no DNA, so they cannot vary
Sugarcane reproduces asexually, so its DNA is copied with only tiny errors, while sexual reproduction in humans mixes DNA from two parents
Humans reproduce asexually, which creates more variation
Sugarcane plants do not copy their DNA when they reproduce, so nothing can change

hint: Think about how many parents each type of offspring has.
explanation: In **asexual reproduction** (sugarcane) the only variation comes from small inaccuracies in DNA copying, so the plants are nearly identical. **Sexual reproduction** (humans) combines DNA from two parents, so it produces far greater diversity. Sugarcane certainly has DNA, and humans do not reproduce asexually.

subject: biology
prompt: A species reproduces asexually. Trait A is seen in 10% of its members and trait B in 60%. Which trait most likely appeared earlier?

image.alt: A family tree showing one organism giving rise to more and more varied descendants over generations

options.text: Trait B, because it has had more generations in which to be copied and spread
Trait A, because a rarer trait must be older
Both arose at the same time
Trait A, because rare traits are stronger

hint: A trait passes to the descendants of the individual that first had it.
explanation: Variations are inherited, so each new generation carries the differences of its parents plus new ones. A trait found in **more** individuals has had **more generations** to spread, so trait **B** is likely older. Rarity does not mean age or strength.

subject: biology
prompt: A bacterium divides into two cells. These two cells divide again, giving four bacteria. The four bacteria are very similar but not exactly the same. Why?

image.alt: One bacterium dividing twice into four nearly identical bacteria

options.text: Two different parents contributed DNA to each cell
Bacteria do not copy their DNA before dividing
Sexual reproduction happens between the two divisions
Small inaccuracies creep in when the DNA is copied

hint: Division by one cell is asexual. Where can differences still come from?
explanation: Even in **asexual reproduction** the DNA copying is not perfect. Tiny **inaccuracies in DNA copying** produce minor differences between the four bacteria. There is only one parent, and DNA is copied before every division, so the other options are wrong.

subject: biology
prompt: During a heat wave, most bacteria in a colony die. But a few of them survive and multiply. How do variations help the species here?

image.alt: A heat wave kills some bacteria while heat-tolerant ones survive

options.text: Heat makes every bacterium change its DNA to cope
Variation lets every individual survive equally well
Heat-tolerant variants have an advantage, survive, and pass the trait to the next generation
Variations are never inherited by the next generation

hint: Think about which individuals are left to reproduce.
explanation: Some bacteria happen to carry a variation that lets them **withstand heat**. They survive and reproduce, so the species continues. Selection of variants by environmental factors forms the basis of **evolution**. Variations arise by chance beforehand; heat does not create them to order.

subject: biology
prompt: Select all the correct statements about variation.

image.alt: A family tree showing growing differences over generations

options.text: Even asexual reproduction produces a little variation, because DNA copying is slightly inaccurate
Sexual reproduction produces greater diversity than asexual reproduction
All variants have an equal chance of surviving in any environment
Each generation inherits the differences of its parents and adds new ones
Selection of variants by the environment forms the basis of evolutionary processes

hint: Think of the heat-wave example: do all bacteria fare equally well?
explanation: True: copying errors (asexual), greater diversity from sexual reproduction, inheritance plus new differences each generation, and selection by the environment as the basis of evolution. **False:** variants do **not** have equal chances. A heat-tolerant bacterium does well in a heat wave and a heat-sensitive one does not.

subject: biology
prompt: There are 40 students in a class. 30 of them have free earlobes and the others have attached earlobes. What percentage of the students have attached earlobes?

image.alt: Side views of a head with a free earlobe and a head with an attached earlobe

hint: First find how many students have attached earlobes.
explanation: Attached = $40 - 30 = 10$ students, so $\dfrac{10}{40} \times 100 = 25\%$. 75% is the **free** earlobe group, 30% is just the number of students with free lobes, and 10% is a head-count, not a percentage.

subject: biology

options.text: Picture B

explanation: In an **attached** earlobe the lowest part of the ear is closely joined to the side of the head. In a **free** earlobe the lobe hangs loose below the ear (Picture A).

subject: biology
prompt: Mendel crossed a tall pea plant with a short pea plant. What did he find in the first (F1) generation?

image.alt: A tall and a short pea plant crossed giving three tall F1 plants

options.text: All the plants were tall; there were no medium-height plants
All the plants were medium in height
Half were tall and half were short
All the plants were short

hint: Was there any blending of the two heights?
explanation: All F1 plants were **tall**, with no halfway (medium) plants. Only **one** of the parental traits was seen, so the traits do not blend.

subject: biology
prompt: Read the Assertion (A) and Reason (R) carefully.

image.alt: F1 tall plants self-pollinate to give three tall and one short F2 plants

assertion: Short plants appear again in the F2 generation, even though all the F1 plants were tall.
reason: Each F1 plant has two different copies of the height gene. The copy for shortness is present, but it is not expressed (it does not show).
hint: Where was the shortness trait hiding?
explanation: Both **A and R are true and R explains A**. F1 plants are Tt. They show tallness because T is dominant, but they still carry t. When they self-pollinate, some F2 plants receive two copies of t and are short (about one quarter).

subject: biology
prompt: Tall F1 plants were self-pollinated, and 1200 F2 plants were produced. About how many of these would be short?

image.alt: F1 tall plants self-pollinate to give three tall and one short F2 plants

hint: Recall the ratio of tall to short plants that Mendel found in the F2 generation.
explanation: The F2 ratio is **3 tall : 1 short**, so short plants are $\dfrac{1}{4} \times 1200 = 300$. 900 is the number of **tall** plants, 600 wrongly takes half, and 400 wrongly takes one third.

subject: biology
prompt: Tap a **short** plant of the **F2** generation.

image.alt: Pea plants of the P generation, F1 generation and F2 generation

hint: Find the F2 group first, then compare the stem heights within it.
explanation: The F2 generation is the last group. Three of its four plants are tall and one is **short** (genotype tt). The short plant in the P generation is a parent, not an F2 offspring.

subject: biology
prompt: This Punnett square is for the cross $Tt \times Tt$. Tap the box that shows a **short** plant (tt).

image.alt: Punnett square for a cross of two Tt plants showing only the gene combinations in each box

hint: A short plant must have two copies of the recessive gene.
explanation: Only the box with **tt** (one t from each parent) shows a short plant. TT and Tt both show tallness, because one copy of T is enough.

subject: biology
prompt: Tap the box that has **two identical tallness genes** (TT).

image.alt: Punnett square for a cross of two Tt plants showing only the gene combinations in each box

hint: Both letters must be capital T.
explanation: The **TT** box has received T from each parent. Tt boxes are also tall but carry one hidden t, so only TT has two identical tallness genes.

subject: biology
prompt: Match each gene combination with the plant it produces.

image.alt: Gene cards TT, Tt and tt above two tall plants and one short plant

right.text: Tall, with two copies of T
Tall, but carrying a hidden t
Short, with two copies of t

hint: A single T is enough to make the plant tall.
explanation: **TT** is tall with two copies of T. **Tt** is also tall because T is **dominant**, but the recessive t is still carried. **tt** is short, because both copies must be t for the recessive trait to show.

subject: biology
prompt: Select all the correct statements about the height gene (T = tall, t = short) in pea plants.

image.alt: A tall and a short pea plant crossed giving three tall F1 plants

options.text: A single copy of T is enough to make the plant tall
Both copies must be t for the plant to be short
A Tt plant grows to a medium height
A Tt plant carries both the tall and the short factor but expresses only tallness
The trait t is dominant

hint: No blending was seen: F1 plants were tall, not medium.
explanation: **T** is dominant, so one copy gives tallness; the recessive **t** shows only when both copies are t. Tt plants are **tall**, not medium, and carry a hidden t. Calling t dominant is wrong, since it is hidden in Tt.

subject: biology
prompt: Match each cross with the ratio of **offspring types** you expect. (T = tall, R = round, Y = yellow)

image.alt: Punnett square for a cross of two Tt plants

hint: Draw a Punnett square for each cross.
explanation: TT × tt gives only Tt, so **all tall**. Tt × Tt gives TT, Tt, Tt, tt, so **3 tall : 1 short**. Tt × tt gives Tt, Tt, tt, tt, so **1 : 1**. A dihybrid cross of two Rr Yy plants gives the **9 : 3 : 3 : 1** ratio.

subject: biology
prompt: A tall plant with genotype Tt is crossed with a short plant (tt). What ratio of tall to short offspring do you expect?

image.alt: Punnett square for a cross of Tt with tt

options.text: 3 tall : 1 short
All tall
1 tall : 3 short
1 tall : 1 short

hint: Gametes of Tt are T and t. Gametes of tt are all t.
explanation: The Tt parent makes T and t gametes, and the tt parent makes only t. The four boxes are Tt, tt, Tt, tt, so half the offspring are tall and half are short: **1 : 1**. The 3 : 1 ratio belongs to Tt × Tt, not to this cross.

subject: biology
prompt: Put the steps of Mendel's pea-plant experiment in order.

image.alt: A tall and a short pea plant crossed giving three tall F1 plants

items.text: Count the F2 plants: about 3 tall for every 1 short
Cross a tall pea plant with a short pea plant
Let the F1 plants self-pollinate to get F2 plants
Conclude that tallness is dominant and shortness is recessive
Observe that all F1 plants are tall

hint: F1 comes before F2.
explanation: Mendel first **crossed** tall and short parents, saw that **all F1** were tall, let F1 **self-pollinate**, **counted** the F2 progeny, and so reached the idea of dominant and recessive traits.

subject: biology
prompt: In a Mendelian cross, a tall plant with violet flowers was crossed with a short plant with white flowers. All the progeny (offspring) had violet flowers, but almost half of them were short. What is the genetic make-up of the tall parent?

image.alt: A tall violet pea plant crossed with a short white one giving violet flowers with tall and short plants

options.text: TTWW
TTww
TtWW
TtWw

hint: Treat height and flower colour one at a time. The short white parent is ttww.
explanation: **Flower colour:** all progeny are violet, so the tall parent has only W (WW). If it were Ww, about half the progeny would be white. **Height:** about half are short, so the tall parent has one t, which means Tt. A TT parent would give all tall plants. Hence **TtWW**.

subject: biology
prompt: A man with blood group A marries a woman with blood group O. Their daughter has blood group O. Is this information enough to tell which trait, A or O, is dominant?

image.alt: A family tree with a father of blood group A, a mother of group O and a daughter of group O

options.text: Yes, A is dominant because the father has it
Yes, O is dominant because the daughter has it
No, because blood group is not an inherited trait
No, because the information fits either A or O being dominant

hint: Try each possibility in turn and see whether the family could still arise.
explanation: Try both possibilities. If **A is dominant**, the father is A with a hidden O copy (AO), the mother is OO, and the daughter received O from each parent (OO). If **O is dominant**, the father must be AA; the daughter received A from him and O from her mother (AO) and shows O because O is dominant. Both stories fit the facts, so this family alone cannot tell us which trait is dominant (using the simple dominant/recessive model of the chapter).

subject: biology
prompt: A study found that children with light-coloured eyes often have parents who also have light-coloured eyes. From this, can we say whether light eye colour is dominant or recessive?

image.alt: Two light-eyed parents and their light-eyed children

options.text: No, this pattern alone fits both possibilities, so more crosses would be needed
Yes, it is dominant because parents pass it on
Yes, it is recessive because it needs both parents
No, because eye colour is not inherited

hint: Would the same pattern appear if the trait were dominant?
explanation: Parents often pass on a trait whether it is dominant or recessive, so the pattern does not reveal which. To decide, you would need a cross between **contrasting** parents (for example light-eyed and dark-eyed) and a look at the **first-generation** children.

subject: biology
prompt: Which plan is the best way to find out the **dominant coat colour** in dogs?

image.alt: A black dog and a brown dog and four puppies of unknown colour

options.text: Count the black and brown dogs in a town: the commoner colour is dominant
Cross a pure black dog with a pure brown dog and note the colour of all the first-generation puppies
Breed two black dogs together and count the puppies
Compare the weights of black and brown dogs

hint: Mendel crossed plants with contrasting traits and looked at the F1.
explanation: Following Mendel, cross dogs with **contrasting pure** coat colours. The colour that appears in all the first-generation puppies is the **dominant** one. How common a colour is does not show dominance, and counting puppies or comparing weights says nothing about colour.

subject: biology
prompt: Read the Assertion (A) and Reason (R) carefully.

image.alt: A notebook with tally marks counting tall and short pea plants and a pencil

assertion: Mendel was able to discover the 3 : 1 pattern in his F2 pea plants.
reason: He was the first to count how many plants showed each trait in every generation.
hint: Why did counting help?
explanation: Both are true and R explains A. Earlier scientists studied inheritance but did not **count**. Mendel combined his knowledge of science and **mathematics**, counted each trait in every generation, and so found the ratios.

subject: biology
prompt: Round green seeds (RRyy) are crossed with wrinkled yellow seeds (rrYY). All the F1 seeds are round and yellow. Select the **dominant** traits.

image.alt: Four pea seed types: round yellow, round green, wrinkled yellow and wrinkled green

options.text: Round seed shape
Wrinkled seed shape
Yellow seed colour
Green seed colour

hint: The dominant traits are the ones seen in the F1.
explanation: The F1 seeds (Rr Yy) are all **round and yellow**, so these traits are dominant. Wrinkled and green are hidden in the F1 and return only in F2, so they are recessive.

subject: biology
prompt: Round green seeds (RRyy) are crossed with wrinkled yellow seeds (rrYY). Which pair of F2 seed types are **new combinations** that neither parent had?

options.text: Picture A

image.alt: A round green seed and a wrinkled yellow seed

options.text: Picture B

image.alt: A round yellow seed and a round green seed

options.text: Picture C

image.alt: A round yellow seed and a wrinkled green seed

options.text: Picture D

image.alt: A wrinkled yellow seed and a wrinkled green seed

hint: Parents were round green and wrinkled yellow. Which two types did neither parent show?
explanation: The parents were **round green** and **wrinkled yellow** (Picture A). The new F2 combinations are **round yellow** and **wrinkled green**. This shows seed shape and seed colour are inherited independently. Pictures B and D each contain one parental type.

subject: biology
prompt: Look at the 16-box Punnett square for $Rr\,Yy \times Rr\,Yy$. How many boxes show **round, yellow** seeds?

image.alt: Sixteen-box Punnett square for a dihybrid cross of round yellow seeds

hint: A seed needs at least one R and at least one Y.
explanation: Round yellow needs R and Y at least once: $9$ boxes. The ratio is $9 : 3 : 3 : 1$ (round yellow : round green : wrinkled yellow : wrinkled green). 12 is the number of **round** seeds overall (9 yellow plus 3 green), 3 is one of the smaller classes, and 4 is just the number of gamete types.

subject: biology
prompt: Tap the box showing **wrinkled, green** seeds (rryy).

image.alt: Sixteen-box Punnett square for a dihybrid cross of round yellow seeds

hint: Both traits must be recessive, so every letter is lower case.
explanation: Wrinkled needs two r, and green needs two y, so the genotype is **rryy**. It appears only once in 16 boxes (bottom right). Rryy is round green, RRyy is round green, and rrYY is wrinkled yellow.

subject: biology
prompt: You cross $Rr\,Yy \times Rr\,Yy$ and collect 1600 F2 seeds. About how many of them do you expect to be **wrinkled and green**?

image.alt: Bar chart of 315 round yellow, 108 round green, 101 wrinkled yellow and 32 wrinkled green seeds

hint: Count how many of the 16 boxes are rryy, then take that fraction of 1600.
explanation: Wrinkled green is $\dfrac{1}{16}$ of the seeds: $\dfrac{1600}{16} = 100$. The 300 uses $\dfrac{3}{16}$ (a single-recessive class), 400 uses $\dfrac{1}{4}$, and 900 uses $\dfrac{9}{16}$ (round yellow).

subject: biology
prompt: Mendel counted the F2 seeds of each type. Arrange the seed types from the **most** seeds to the **fewest** seeds.

image.alt: Four pea seed types: round yellow, round green, wrinkled yellow and wrinkled green

items.text: Wrinkled, green
Round, yellow
Wrinkled, yellow
Round, green

hint: The ratio is 9 : 3 : 3 : 1.
explanation: Mendel counted **315** round yellow, **108** round green, **101** wrinkled yellow and **32** wrinkled green seeds out of 556. This is close to the 9 : 3 : 3 : 1 ratio.

subject: biology
prompt: Match each F2 seed type with the number Mendel counted (out of 556 seeds).

image.alt: Four pea seed types: round yellow, round green, wrinkled yellow and wrinkled green

hint: The biggest class has both dominant traits; the smallest has both recessive.
explanation: The counts were 315 (round yellow), 108 (round green), 101 (wrinkled yellow) and 32 (wrinkled green). Round yellow is the biggest group because it shows two dominant traits, and wrinkled green is the smallest because it needs two recessive traits.

subject: biology
prompt: Read the Assertion (A) and Reason (R) carefully.

image.alt: A Rr Yy parent cell makes four kinds of gamete RY, Ry, rY and ry

assertion: In Mendel's dihybrid cross, some F2 plants showed new combinations of traits, such as tall with wrinkled seeds.
reason: The genes for different traits are inherited independently of each other.
hint: If traits always travelled together, new combinations could not appear.
explanation: Both are true and R explains A. Because the genes for two traits are inherited **independently**, they can be **recombined** in the gametes (RY, Ry, rY, ry), and the F2 offspring show new trait combinations.

subject: biology
prompt: A pea plant with genotype $Rr\,Yy$ makes gametes. Which of these can **not** be a gamete?

image.alt: A Rr Yy parent cell makes four kinds of gamete RY, Ry, rY and ry

options.text: RY
rY
Ry
Rr

hint: A gamete gets only one copy of each gene.
explanation: A gamete carries **one** copy of each gene: R or r, and Y or y. The possible gametes are **RY, Ry, rY, ry**. Rr has both copies of the same gene, which no gamete can hold.

subject: biology
prompt: Select all the correct statements about chromosomes and germ cells.

image.alt: A body cell with two pairs of chromosomes makes four germ cells with one chromosome from each pair

options.text: Every germ cell takes one chromosome from each pair
A chromosome in a germ cell may be of maternal or paternal origin
Each germ cell carries both copies of every chromosome
When two germ cells combine, the normal number of chromosomes is restored
The gene set is a single long thread of DNA

hint: Each cell has two copies; each germ cell has only one.
explanation: Each gene set is packaged as **separate, independent chromosomes**. A body cell has two copies of each, and each germ cell takes **one** of each pair (maternal or paternal). Fusion of two germ cells restores the normal number. A germ cell does not carry both copies, and the gene set is not one long thread.

subject: biology
prompt: Read the Assertion (A) and Reason (R) carefully.

image.alt: An egg and a sperm each with one chromosome set fuse to give a zygote with two sets

assertion: A human germ cell has the same number of chromosomes as a body cell.
reason: Fertilisation brings the number of chromosomes in the zygote back to normal.
hint: Count the sets in the egg, the sperm and the zygote.
explanation: A is **false**: a germ cell has only **one** chromosome of each pair, so half the number found in a body cell. R is **true**: when the egg and sperm combine, the zygote again has two sets, which keeps the DNA of the species stable.

subject: biology
prompt: Match each term with its meaning.

image.alt: Zoom from a cell with a nucleus to a chromosome to a DNA helix with a highlighted gene

right.text: A section of DNA that gives information for one protein
A separate, independent piece in which a gene set is packaged
Expressed even when only one copy is present
Expressed only when both copies are the recessive version

hint: A gene is for one protein; a chromosome holds many genes.
explanation: A **gene** is a section of DNA that gives information for one **protein**. A **chromosome** is one of the independent pieces in which the gene set is packaged. A **dominant** trait needs only one copy to be expressed, while a **recessive** trait is expressed only when both copies are the recessive version.

items.text: Gene
Nucleus
DNA molecule
Chromosome

explanation: The big orange X-shaped body is a **chromosome**. The nucleus holds chromosomes, DNA is the thread that makes them up, and the highlighted piece of DNA is one **gene**.

subject: biology

image.alt: Chain from a gene to an enzyme to a plant hormone to a tall plant

hint: The gene gives the instructions to make this protein, and it is a middle step.
explanation: The gene gives the information to make an **enzyme** (a protein). If the enzyme works efficiently, a lot of **hormone** is made and the plant grows tall.

subject: biology
prompt: An enzyme helps a plant make its growth hormone. A change in a gene makes this enzyme work less efficiently. What will most likely happen?

image.alt: Chain from a gene to an enzyme to a plant hormone to a tall plant

options.text: Less hormone is made, so the plant is short
More hormone is made, so the plant is tall
The plant stops making all proteins
Nothing changes, because genes do not control traits

hint: Follow the chain: gene, enzyme, hormone, height.
explanation: Genes control traits through **proteins**. A less efficient enzyme makes **less hormone**, so the plant grows **short**. This is how the gene for shortness acts.

subject: biology
prompt: Arrange the steps in order, starting from the gene and ending with the height of the plant.

items.text: Plant growth hormone is made
Gene gives the information for an enzyme
Plant grows tall
Enzyme is made and works efficiently

explanation: The **gene** provides the information, the **enzyme** is made, the enzyme helps make the **hormone**, and the hormone triggers growth so the plant is **tall**.

subject: biology
prompt: Match each item with the way its sex is decided or described.

image.alt: Two thermometers show a cool and a warm nest of reptile eggs

right.text: Temperature at which the eggs are kept
One normal X and one short Y

hint: Humans are XX or XY; the others do not rely on that.
explanation: In some **reptiles** the egg temperature decides the sex. **Snails** can change sex, so sex is not genetically fixed. In humans it is largely **genetic**: women are **XX** and men are **XY** with a short Y.

subject: biology
prompt: Select all the correct statements about sex determination.

image.alt: A snail changes from one sex to the other

options.text: In some reptiles, the temperature of the fertilised eggs decides the sex
Snails can change sex, so sex is not genetically determined in them
In human beings, the genes inherited from the parents largely decide the sex
All species use the same strategy to determine sex
Women have a mismatched pair of sex chromosomes

hint: Different species use very different strategies.
explanation: Some species use **environmental cues** (temperature in some reptiles), snails can **change sex**, and in humans the **inherited genes** largely decide sex. Species do not all use one strategy, and a woman has a perfect pair (**XX**), not a mismatched one.

subject: biology
prompt: Which picture shows the sex chromosomes of a **man**?

image.alt: A single X chromosome

options.text: Picture B

image.alt: Two X chromosomes

options.text: Picture C

image.alt: Two Y chromosomes

options.text: Picture D

image.alt: An X and a short Y chromosome

hint: A man has a mismatched pair.
explanation: Men are **XY**: one normal-sized X and one short **Y** (Picture D). Women are XX (Picture B). Humans have 23 pairs: 22 ordinary pairs plus the sex chromosomes, so a lone X (A) or YY (C) is not a normal pair.

subject: biology
prompt: Tap the **sperm** that will give a **boy** if it fertilises an egg.

image.alt: Diagram of human sex chromosomes: sperm X or Y and eggs with X give XX or XY zygotes

hint: A boy is XY, and the egg always supplies the X.
explanation: A child who inherits a **Y** chromosome from the father is a **boy**. The egg always carries X, so a sperm carrying Y gives **XY**. A sperm carrying X gives XX, a girl.

subject: biology
prompt: Tap the parent who has a **perfect pair** of sex chromosomes (both X).

image.alt: Diagram of human sex chromosomes: sperm X or Y and eggs with X give XX or XY zygotes

hint: Women are XX; men have a mismatched pair.
explanation: A woman has two X chromosomes, so every egg carries an **X**. A man is XY and makes two kinds of sperm, which is why the father decides the sex of the child.

subject: biology
prompt: Read the Assertion (A) and Reason (R) carefully.

image.alt: Diagram of human sex chromosomes showing XX and XY outcomes

assertion: In human beings, a child who inherits a Y chromosome from the father is a boy.
reason: In some reptiles, the temperature at which fertilised eggs are kept decides whether the young are male or female.
hint: Is the second statement the reason for the first?
explanation: Both are true, but R does **not** explain A. In humans the sex is decided by the **chromosome** inherited from the father (Y gives a boy, X a girl). Temperature-dependent sex determination is a different strategy used by some reptiles.

subject: biology
prompt: A couple already has three daughters. What is the chance that their fourth child is a boy?

image.alt: Three daughters and a coin showing X or Y for the fourth child

options.text: 1 in 8
1 in 4
1 in 16

hint: Does what happened in the earlier births change the chances for the next one?
explanation: The father's sperm carries **X or Y with equal chance** every time, whatever happened before. So a boy has a 1 in 2 chance. 1 in 8 is the chance of three girls in a row, and 1 in 16 is the chance of four girls. Past births do not change the next one.

subject: biology
prompt: Arrange in order the events that decide the sex of a child.

image.alt: Diagram of human sex chromosomes showing the egg, sperm and zygote

items.text: The zygote has XX or XY chromosomes
The child develops as a girl (XX) or a boy (XY)
The egg (always X) and sperm (X or Y) are formed
A sperm fuses with the egg

hint: Fertilisation comes between making the gametes and forming the zygote.
explanation: The mother's egg always carries **X**, while the father's sperm carries **X or Y**. Fertilisation produces a zygote that is **XX** (girl) or **XY** (boy), and the child develops accordingly.
